hook: A hiking trail is only usable if every step of it is passable, not just the start and the finish. Calculus asks the same of a function on an interval: it must be continuous at every point along the way. Luckily, most functions you know come with that guarantee on their whole domain.

options: $f(c)$ is defined, $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ exists, and they are equal

prereq.q: What is the domain of $\ln x$?
prereq.why: A logarithm is defined only for positive inputs.

figure.caption: A function and the intervals on which it is continuous.

chain.cause: A function is continuous at every point of an open interval
chain.effect: it is continuous on that interval: its graph has no break there
at the endpoints only the one-sided limit from inside counts: $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$ and $\lim_{x \to b^-} f(x) = f(b)$

chain.cause: Polynomial, rational, root, exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions
chain.effect: are continuous on their domains, so you only check where they are undefined

chain.cause: Continuous functions are combined by sums, products, quotients or composition
chain.effect: the result is continuous wherever it is defined; only break points of piecewise rules need a separate check

ideas: Continuous on an interval: continuous at every point of it. At a closed endpoint, only the one-sided limit from inside must match the value.
Polynomials, $e^x$, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are continuous on $(-\infty, \infty)$.

Rational functions, roots, $\ln x$ and $\tan x$ are continuous on their domains: avoid zeros of denominators, negative inputs to even roots, inputs to $\ln$ that are not positive, and zeros of $\cos x$ for $\tan x$.
Sums, products, quotients (denominator not 0) and compositions of continuous functions are continuous.
For a piecewise function, each piece is handled by the rules above; check each break point with the three conditions.

misconception.wrong: If $f$ is continuous on $(1, 5)$ and on $[5, 8]$, it is continuous on $(1, 8]$.
misconception.right: Continuity on $[5, 8]$ only guarantees continuity from the right at 5. The left-hand limit at 5 can still differ from $f(5)$, so $f$ may jump there. Check the shared point with all three conditions.

summary: A function is continuous on an interval when it is continuous at every point of it, with one-sided continuity at closed endpoints. The familiar function families are continuous on their domains, and sums, products, quotients and compositions keep that. So you only need to check where a function is undefined and where a piecewise rule switches.
